notes:
Scope: researchers, identity-system designers and privacy thinkers whose largely online work shaped the privacy debate on the line that leads to person-held terms — re-identification (Sweeney; Narayanan & Shmatikov), machine-readable notice and the cost of consent (Cranor; McDonald), browser-sent preferences (Soghoian's Do Not Track), design-side and contextual theories (Cavoukian; Nissenbaum; boyd; Zuboff), and the user-centric identity / VRM line (Cameron; Kaliya Young; Searls; Christopher Allen; Berners-Lee's Solid). 15 people, 13 events, 6 myths, 12 openly licensed portraits. Method: one person at a time; every quote was copied from text printed by tools/fetch-text.py and re-checked with --check at the end (114 source objects, all CONFIRMED). Five quotes from Christopher Soghoian's Blogger site and dubfire.net return NOT-FOUND from fetch-text.py only because its paragraph extractor skips div/
text; they were verified against the same fetched HTML's full get_text() and each source note says so. Some PDFs' text layers use 'fi'/'ff' ligatures, which are kept in the quotes so they match. Portrait licences were read from the Commons API extmetadata (and file wikitext where the metadata conflicted); thumbnails are saved as JPEG q82 in assets/media. Corrections to the brief: (1) the first Internet Identity Workshop (26–27 Oct 2005) met in Berkeley (Hillside Club), not Mountain View — IIW moved to the Computer History Museum later (see myth); (2) McDonald & Cranor's published paper gives a point estimate of 244 hours a year to read policies (Table 7) while its conclusion says 'approximately 201 hours' — both are recorded; (3) the Privacy by Design resolution (Jerusalem, 27–29 Oct 2010) is NOT written as an event here because global.json already has it as jerusalem-resolution-privacy-by-design-2010; it is cited in Cavoukian's card. Overlaps for the editorial layer to resolve: latanya-sweeney also appears in personas-code.json and doc-searls in personas-advocates.json; myterms.json has projectvrm-launched-berkman-2006 (duplicate of searls-projectvrm-launched-berkman-2006) and P3P / Do Not Track as lineage items (this file has them as events w3c-p3p-recommendation-2002 and soghoian-stamm-do-not-track-header-prototype-2009). Known gaps: no openly licensed portraits found on Commons for Vitaly Shmatikov, Aleecia McDonald or Christopher Allen; Kim Cameron's portrait is a group photo (with Drummond Reed and Esther Dyson); Kaliya Young's is a wide workshop shot. Cynthia Dwork (differential privacy) and Ashkan Soltani are covered in other persona slices and were not duplicated. The first use of 'VRM' (reportedly a Gillmor Gang podcast, 1 Sept 2006) and the ProjectVRM launch month were not verified — the event is dated 2006 only.

keyWork.title: Simple Demographics Often Identify People Uniquely (Carnegie Mellon University, Data Privacy Working Paper 3)

people.contribution: As an MIT graduate student in 1997, Sweeney linked a $20 Cambridge voter list to Massachusetts state-employee health data released without names, and picked out Governor William Weld's medical records. people.name: Lorrie Faith Cranor
people.roles: computer scientist · usable-privacy researcher · P3P co-author · FTC chief technologist (2016)

keyWork.title: The Platform for Privacy Preferences 1.0 (P3P1.0) Specification, W3C Recommendation (co-author, then at AT&T)

people.contribution: Cranor chaired the W3C working group that wrote P3P and was one of its authors; the standard (Recommendation, 16 April 2002) let websites publish their privacy practices in a machine-readable format for browsers to read on users' behalf. In 2012 she published a candid post-mortem of P3P and of notice-and-choice, and in 2016 she served as chief technologist at the U.S. Federal Trade Commission.
people.quote: P3P is a user empowerment tool that was developed in response to Congressional and FTC interest in online privacy in the mid-1990s and concerns that it was unrealistic to expect consumers to read long online privacy policies at every website they visit.

people.influence: Her post-mortem is a detailed insider's account of why P3P failed: the negotiation protocol was dropped, Internet Explorer's use of compact policies as a cookie gate led thousands of sites to post copied or erroneous policies, and no enforcement followed — lessons W3C itself repeated when it declared P3P obsolete in 2018.
people.thread: P3P's founding idea was a browser that would 'negotiate with websites, and take actions on their users’ behalf' — the idea that person-proffered terms (IEEE 7012) and AI agents now revive. The difference is who states the terms: in P3P the site published its policy and the person's browser evaluated it; in IEEE 7012 the person proffers the terms.

events.title: A graduate student finds the governor in 'anonymous' health data

events.title: ZIP code, gender and birth date: the 87% estimate
events.summary: In a Carnegie Mellon working paper, Latanya Sweeney used 1990 U.S. Census summary data to estimate how many people had rare combinations of demographic values. She found that 87% of the population (216 million of 248 million) likely had a unique combination of five-digit ZIP code, gender and date of birth, and about half (53%) on place, gender and date of birth. A 2006 re-analysis of the 2000 Census by Philippe Golle put the ZIP–gender–birth-date figure at 63%.

events.title: Netflix's 'anonymous' ratings are shown to be re-identifiable
events.place: IEEE Symposium on Security and Privacy, Oakland, California
events.summary: Arvind Narayanan and Vitaly Shmatikov of the University of Texas at Austin presented a statistical attack on the Netflix Prize dataset, which held movie ratings of about 500,000 subscribers with names replaced by numbers. They calculated that eight ratings (two of which may be wrong) with dates accurate to 14 days single out 99% of records. As a proof of concept they compared the public Internet Movie Database ratings of about 50 users with the dataset and matched two of them to their Netflix records with high statistical confidence, uncovering what the authors called apparent political preferences and other potentially sensitive information. In March 2010, after FTC staff raised the research with the company, Netflix suspended plans for a second prize dataset.
events.significance: It carried re-identification from demographics to behaviour — what people watch, click and buy — the very data online services collect, and it moved a regulator to act.

events.title: A browser header that says 'do not track'
events.place: Future of Privacy Forum meeting and conference call (FPF is based in Washington, D.C.)
events.summary: In July 2009 Christopher Soghoian and Sid Stamm built a prototype Firefox add-on that added 'X-Do-Not-Track: 1' and 'X-Behavioral-Ad-Opt-Out: 1' headers to outgoing web requests, as an alternative to the per-company opt-out cookies that were erased whenever users cleared their cookies. In mid-July Soghoian pitched the header at a meeting and conference call organised by the Future of Privacy Forum; none of the advertising firms showed interest, and after joining the FTC a couple of months later he decided against adding the header to his TACO opt-out add-on. After FTC chairman Jon Leibowitz revived the 'do not track' idea in July 2010, the header approach displaced a 2007 advocacy proposal for an FTC-compiled Do Not Track list, and W3C worked on it as the DNT standard until 2019.
events.significance: It moved the tracking choice from one cookie per ad company to a single signal a person's own software sends to every site: the one-bit ancestor of machine-readable personal terms.

events.title: Reading every privacy policy would take 244 hours a year
events.summary: Aleecia McDonald and Lorrie Faith Cranor of Carnegie Mellon measured how long privacy policies take to read and skim and multiplied by the number of sites Americans visit. Their point estimate was 244 hours a year per person to read the policy of each new site word-for-word — about 40 minutes a day — worth about $781 billion a year nationally in lost time. The paper's conclusion gives a lower figure of about 201 hours, which does not match its own tables.
events.significance: It put a number on why notice-and-consent fails: no one can read the terms, so the terms have to be read by machines — or set by the person.

events.title: TrackMeNot hides real searches in a cloud of decoys
events.place: New York University, New York City
events.summary: Daniel Howe and Helen Nissenbaum of New York University released TrackMeNot, a free Firefox extension that periodically sends randomised 'ghost' queries to search engines so that a user's real searches are harder to profile. Its authors cited the U.S. Justice Department's 2005 subpoena to Google for search records and the New York Times coverage of AOL's release of search logs. myths.claim: 87% of Americans can be identified from just their ZIP code, gender and date of birth.
myths.correction: Sweeney's 87% was an estimate from 1990 Census summary data of how many people 'likely' had a unique combination of five-digit ZIP, gender and birth date — not a count of people actually re-identified. Re-running the analysis on the 2000 Census, Philippe Golle found 63%. Actually naming someone also needs an outside list (such as a voter roll) that contains them; Barth-Jones argues that incomplete lists make many such matches uncertain. The core point — that a few ordinary attributes single out most people — survived the re-analysis.

myths.claim: Christopher Soghoian invented Do Not Track, an anti-tracking tool that all major browsers use.
myths.correction: By Soghoian's own account the name came from a 2007 proposal by public-interest groups for an FTC-run 'Do Not Track list'; the idea of a browser header had been urged on him by Dan Kaminsky and Mozilla's Mike Shaver before he and Sid Stamm built the first header prototype in July 2009. DNT was a request, not a blocking tool: it only worked if sites chose to honour it, W3C closed the standard in January 2019 for lack of deployment, and in February 2019 Apple began removing it from Safari because the signal could itself be used to fingerprint users.

myths.claim: OAuth was created at the Internet Identity Workshop.
myths.correction: Speaker biographies often say OAuth and OpenID Connect were 'created' at IIW. OAuth's own published history says it 'started around November 2006', while Twitter's Blaine Cook was working on an OpenID implementation. He, Chris Messina, Ma.gnolia's Larry Halff, David Recordon and others then met at a CitizenSpace OpenID meeting. A Google group followed in April 2007, and the final draft of OAuth Core 1.0 was released on 3 October 2007. That history does not mention IIW. IIW co-founder Phil Windley's own, more careful wording is that IIW 'gave us space to define' protocols such as OAuth. That makes IIW a forum where the work was discussed and advanced, not the place where it began.

myths.claim: Young people who grew up online don't care about privacy.
myths.correction: Teens did share more about themselves as platforms grew — Pew found each of five kinds of personal information more widely posted in 2012 than in 2006 — but few took a fully public approach. myths.claim: Shoshana Zuboff coined the term 'surveillance capitalism'.
myths.correction: Zuboff developed the best-known theory of surveillance capitalism and made the term famous with her 2019 book, and reviewers often credit her with coining it. She set out the concept in a Frankfurter Allgemeine Zeitung essay published on 15 September 2014. But about two months earlier, John Bellamy Foster and Robert W. McChesney had published 'Surveillance Capitalism: Monopoly-Finance Capital, the Military-Industrial Complex, and the Digital Age' in the July–August 2014 issue of the socialist magazine Monthly Review. Their analysis was different, centred on monopoly capital and the military-industrial complex. The phrase has more than one origin; Zuboff's meaning, the extraction of behavioural data to sell predictions, is her own.
